newsitem.title: USA: Bush backs Albright bipartisan U.S. foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Bush backs Albright bipartisan U.S. foreign policy.

text.p: Former President George Bush on Saturday threw his weight behind the Clinton administration's bid for a bipartisan foreign policy, taking issue with Republican colleagues over chemical weapons and foreign spending.

At a breakfast with new Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Bush warmly applauded her efforts to get a global chemical weapons ban ratified by the Senate, to raise the foreign affairs budget and pay arrears to the United Nations.
"I told the secretary that she would have my enthusiastic support in her quest for bipartisanship in foreign policy," Bush told reporters outside his home in a residential compound in Houston.

"I told her I would strongly support her efforts to get this chemical weapons treaty approved," he said. "I think it is vitally important for the United States to be out front, not to be dragged kicking and screaming to the finish line."

Bush and his Secretary of State James Baker played a key role during in getting the treaty -- which bans production, stockpiling and use of posion gas -- negotiated and signed in Paris in January 1993.

But conservative Republicans such as Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms have held up ratification, saying the treaty is ineffectual, will not bind "rogue states" and will burden the U.S. chemical industry.

The Democratic administration has launched an effort to get the pact ratified by its entry into force date of April 29, failing which Washington will be barred from administering the treaty. The issue was a key theme of Albright's first policy speech on Friday at Houston's Rice University.

Asked if he would press Helms directly on the issue, Bush said he was "out of the lobbying business," but added: "I hope he listens to what I've said today." Some Republicans support the treaty and Bush's comments were seen as likely to sway waverers.

Albright said President Bill Clinton would be very pleased with Bush's support. She also received strong backing on Friday from Baker, marking a notable success for her first trip outside Washington since she was sworn in Jan. 23.
Bush also attacked what he called the "stupid feeling in some quarters" that the United States had no further foreign policy concerns following the end of the Cold War.

"I hope that Congress will do what's right on a bipartisan basis in terms of proper levels of funding ... these arguments that we ought to cut back on spending for foreign affairs I think is very short-sighted," he said.
"We do that at our own risk for generations to come," he added.
The White House earlier this week sent Congress a budget that includes a request for a 7 percent increase in foreign affairs spending, following a decade of declines.

Bush, who like Albright is a former U.N. ambassador, also backed her demand that the United States should pay more than $1 billion that it owes to the world body. Congress has withheld the funds, accusing the organisation of mismanagement.
"I think it is of fundamental importance with the new change (of secretary-general) at the U.N. that we fulfil our obligations there," he said.
The administration is asking Congress to appropriate the bulk of the money for payment to the United Nations in 1999 if certain conditions are met.
